title: Thirteen Colonies
bigQuestion: How did land, work and law shape life in the thirteen colonies, and who was free?

story.title: Two Mornings in 1740
story.kicker: Same sunrise, same king, same year. Two children wake up to very different days.
paragraphs: The sun comes up over a farm near Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Anna, age nine, hears the rooster before she opens her eyes. Her father is already outside with the cows. Her mother is stirring a pot of cornmeal mush. Anna pulls on her wool dress and goes to gather eggs. The barn smells like hay and cold air.

After breakfast Anna's older brother walks to the mill with a sack of wheat. Anna churns butter until her arms ache. Later her mother will teach her to read from the family Bible. Nobody in the house is rich. But the land is theirs, and the food on the table is food they grew.

Five hundred miles south, the sun comes up over a rice plantation near Charleston, South Carolina. Cato, age nine, wakes on a dirt floor in a small wooden cabin. His mother is already gone to the fields. The rice fields are wet and full of mosquitoes. Cato's job is to scare birds from the young plants.

Cato was born on this plantation. His grandmother was born in Africa. She was taken across the ocean on a ship, chained below the deck. Cato and his family cannot leave. They are not paid. A man who lives in the big house says he owns them. No law in South Carolina says he is wrong.

Anna and Cato will never meet. But they live in the same British colonies, under the same king, in the same year. Their mornings show a hard truth. In the colonies, where you were born, and to whom, decided almost everything about your life.
story.think: Anna and Cato both work hard. What is the biggest difference between their mornings? Why does it matter?

lessons.title: New England: Rocky Soil, Busy Harbors
lessons.mainIdea: New England's thin soil and good harbors pushed people toward fishing, shipbuilding and trade.
reading: A *colony* is a place ruled by a faraway country. By the 1730s, Britain had thirteen colonies along the Atlantic coast. The four northern ones were called New England: Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut and Rhode Island. Winters were long and cold. The soil was thin and full of rocks.

Farmers in New England could feed their families, but not much more. So many people turned to the sea. Cod fish were thick off the coast. Tall forests gave wood for ships. Boston became a busy *harbor*, a safe place where ships load and unload. Ships from Boston carried fish, lumber and rum across the ocean.

We know this from ship records, tax lists and letters. A merchant's account book from Boston lists barrels of fish sent to Spain and the West Indies. Geography did not force people to fish. But it made fishing and trade the smart choice. That is how land shapes life.

words.d: a place that is settled and ruled by a faraway country
a sheltered place on a coast where ships can safely load and unload

look.title: A Field Full of Rocks
look.text: Picture a New England farmer in 1730. He drags a wooden plow through the field. Clunk. Another rock. He digs it out and carries it to the edge. By fall, the edge of his field is a stone wall as high as his waist. Many of these walls still stand in Massachusetts today.
look.prompt: What does the stone wall tell you about farming in New England? Why might a son from this farm choose to become a sailor?

check.q: What is a colony?
choices: A place ruled by a faraway country
A large city by the sea
check.why: A colony is a settlement ruled by a distant country. The thirteen colonies were ruled by Britain.

check.q: Why did many New Englanders fish and build ships instead of just farming?
choices: The soil was rocky and the sea was rich
There were no forests for wood
check.why: Thin, rocky soil made big farms hard. Cod and tall forests made fishing and shipbuilding a better choice.

check.q: Which colony was part of New England?
check.why: New England was Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut and Rhode Island.

lessons.title: The Middle Colonies: Breadbasket
lessons.mainIdea: Rich soil and wide rivers made the Middle Colonies grow grain and welcome many kinds of people.
reading: South of New England lay the Middle Colonies: New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware. Here the soil was deep and dark. Winters were shorter. Farmers grew so much wheat, corn and rye that people called this region the *breadbasket* of the colonies. Anna's family in the story lived here.

Two big rivers, the Hudson and the Delaware, worked like highways. Farmers floated grain to New York City and Philadelphia. Mills along the rivers ground wheat into flour. By 1750, Philadelphia was one of the largest cities in the colonies. Its streets were laid out in a neat grid.

The Middle Colonies were also the most mixed. Pennsylvania was started in 1681 by William Penn, a *Quaker*. Quakers believed every person had a light from God inside. Penn promised freedom of worship. Germans, Dutch, Scots-Irish, Swedes and English all came. On one street in Philadelphia, you might hear four languages.

words.d: a region that grows lots of grain to feed other places
a member of a Christian group that believed in peace and equal worth of every person

look.title: Colonial Cities, About 1760
look.prompt: Which region had two of the three biggest cities? What about that region might explain it?

check.q: Why were the Middle Colonies called the breadbasket?
choices: They grew large amounts of grain
check.why: Deep soil and a milder climate let farmers grow lots of wheat, corn and rye.

check.q: How did the Hudson and Delaware rivers help farmers?
choices: They carried grain to big cities
They powered ships across the ocean
check.why: Rivers acted like highways. Farmers floated grain to markets in New York and Philadelphia.

check.q: What did William Penn promise people who came to Pennsylvania?
check.why: Penn was a Quaker. He welcomed people of many faiths, so many groups moved to Pennsylvania.

lessons.title: The Southern Colonies: Cash Crops
lessons.mainIdea: Warm weather and rich lowlands let the Southern Colonies grow crops to sell, using enslaved labor.
reading: The Southern Colonies were Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. Summers were long and hot. Rivers ran slow through flat, wet land. This was perfect for *cash crops*, crops grown to sell rather than eat. Virginia and Maryland grew tobacco. South Carolina grew rice and indigo, a plant used for blue dye.

A large farm that grew cash crops was called a *plantation*. Tobacco and rice took huge amounts of hand labor. Planters wanted workers who could not quit. So they bought enslaved Africans. By 1740, more than half the people in South Carolina were enslaved. Cato in the story was one of them.

There were few big cities in the South. Charleston was the main one. Most people lived spread out on farms. Rich planters lived in brick houses and sent their sons to England for school. Small farmers lived in one-room cabins. We know the numbers from colonial tax lists, which counted enslaved people as property.

words.d: a crop grown to sell for money, not to eat at home
a large farm that grows one main crop to sell, often using enslaved workers

look.title: Three Maps in One
look.text: Imagine a map of the coast. In the north, forests and rocky shores. In the middle, wide rivers and dark fields. In the south, hot, flat, swampy lowlands near the sea. Now imagine a second map showing what each place shipped out: fish and ships, flour, tobacco and rice.
look.prompt: Match each product to its region. How does the land explain the product?

check.q: What is a cash crop?
choices: A crop grown to feed the family
A crop that grows only in the north
A crop paid for with coins
check.why: Cash crops like tobacco and rice were grown to be sold, often across the ocean.

check.q: Why did planters in the South buy enslaved workers?
choices: Cash crops needed lots of labor and planters wanted workers who could not quit
The soil was too rocky to farm
check.why: Tobacco and rice needed huge hand labor. Planters chose slavery because enslaved people could not leave.

check.q: Which crop was grown mainly in South Carolina?
check.why: South Carolina's hot, wet lowlands were suited to rice and indigo.

lessons.title: Farms, Towns, Ships and Shops
lessons.mainIdea: Most colonists farmed, but towns held the shops, mills and docks that connected farms to the world.
reading: About nine out of ten colonists lived on farms. A farm family made most of what it used. They grew food, spun wool, made soap and candles. But no farm could make everything. For nails, salt, cloth and tools, families went to town.

A colonial town had a blacksmith who shaped iron, a miller who ground grain and a cooper who made barrels. A *merchant* bought and sold goods from far away. In port towns, ships brought tea, sugar and cloth. They left with fish, flour, tobacco and lumber.

Trade connected everyone. A Pennsylvania farmer's wheat became bread in the West Indies. Sugar from there became rum in Rhode Island. Enslaved people were bought and sold in this same trade. A Boston merchant's ledger from the 1700s shows all of it on one page: barrels of rum, bolts of cloth and human beings.

words.d: a person who buys and sells goods, often from far away
a worker who heats and hammers iron into tools, nails and horseshoes

look.title: Market Day
look.text: It is market day in a river town in 1745. A farmer's wagon creaks in with sacks of wheat. At the mill, the great stone wheel grinds. A cooper hammers hoops on a barrel. Down at the dock, a ship unloads barrels of molasses. Sailors shout. A merchant writes in his book.
look.prompt: Trace one sack of wheat from the wagon to a ship. Who touches it along the way?

check.q: Where did most colonists live?
check.why: About nine of ten colonists lived and worked on farms.

check.q: What did a merchant do?
check.why: A merchant traded goods. Coopers made barrels, millers ground grain and blacksmiths worked iron.

check.q: What does the Boston ledger show about colonial trade?
choices: Trade was mostly within one town
Goods and enslaved people were part of the same trade
check.why: The same trade that moved rum and cloth also bought and sold human beings.

lessons.title: A Colonial Child's Day
lessons.mainIdea: Colonial children worked from a young age, and their jobs depended on where they lived and who they were.
reading: There was no such thing as a lazy morning. Colonial children worked. On a farm, a six-year-old fed chickens and carried water. By ten, boys plowed and girls spun thread. Anna churned butter. A girl might sew a *sampler*, a cloth stitched with letters to practice sewing and reading.

In towns, a boy of twelve might become an *apprentice*. He lived with a craftsman for several years and learned the trade. Benjamin Franklin was an apprentice in his brother's print shop in Boston in the 1720s. Girls learned cooking, spinning and child care at home.

Enslaved children worked too, but for no wage and no future choice. Cato scared birds from rice. Older children carried water to field workers. They could be sold away from their parents at any time. Free and enslaved children might live a mile apart and have completely different lives.

words.d: a young person who lives with a skilled worker for years to learn a trade
a piece of cloth stitched with letters and pictures to practice sewing

look.title: Chores by Age on a Farm
look.cite: general pattern from colonial diaries and account books
look.prompt: How do these jobs compare to what you do at your age? What would be hardest?

check.q: What was an apprentice?
choices: A young person learning a trade from a craftsman
A child who did not work
A teacher in a town school
A sailor on a fishing boat
check.why: An apprentice lived with a skilled worker for years to learn a job, like Franklin in the print shop.

check.q: How was an enslaved child's work different from a free farm child's work?
choices: It was for no wage, and the child could be sold away
check.why: Enslaved children were not paid and could be sold away from their families.

check.q: What might a colonial girl learn by sewing a sampler?
check.why: Samplers were stitched with letters, so girls practiced reading and sewing at once.

lessons.title: Church and Schoolhouse
lessons.mainIdea: Religion was central to colonial life, and in New England it led to the first public schools.
reading: In most colonies, the church was the center of town life. In New England, the Puritans built a *meetinghouse* in the middle of each town. Families sat through long sermons on hard benches. In Pennsylvania, Quakers met in plain rooms with no minister. In the South, Anglican churches followed the Church of England.

Puritans believed everyone should read the Bible. So in 1647, Massachusetts passed a law: any town with fifty families had to hire a teacher. Towns with one hundred families needed a grammar school. This was the first law in the colonies requiring schools.

Children learned from a *hornbook*, a wooden paddle with the alphabet under a thin sheet of horn. Later they used the New England Primer, a small book of rhymes and prayers. Outside New England, schooling was spotty. Rich children had tutors. Poor children often had none. Teaching enslaved people to read was against the law in some colonies.

words.d: a plain building in a New England town used for church and town meetings
a wooden paddle with the alphabet on it, covered by a thin clear sheet of horn

look.title: A Rhyme From a Colonial Schoolbook
look.text: The New England Primer taught the alphabet with short rhymes. The letter A went with a rhyme about Adam's fall bringing sin to all people. The letter F went with a picture of an idle fool being whipped at school. Every lesson mixed reading with religion.
look.cite: New England Primer, a colonial schoolbook, early 1700s (described)
look.prompt: What does this schoolbook tell you about what colonists thought school was for?

check.q: What was the main reason Puritans wanted children to learn to read?
check.why: Puritans believed every person should read Scripture, so Massachusetts required towns to hire teachers.

check.q: What did the 1647 Massachusetts law require?
choices: All children to go to college
Towns of fifty families to hire a teacher
Every family to own a Bible
Schools to be free for all colonies
check.why: The law made towns with fifty families hire a teacher. It was the first school law in the colonies.

check.q: Which statement about colonial schooling is true?
choices: Enslaved people were required to attend
Rich children often had tutors while poor children had little schooling
Only the South had public schools
check.why: Outside New England, school depended on money. Some colonies even banned teaching enslaved people to read.

lessons.title: Indentured Servants
lessons.mainIdea: Indentured servants traded years of unpaid work for the trip to America, and then went free.
reading: The trip from Europe cost more than most poor people had. So many signed an *indenture*, a contract. A ship captain or planter paid for the trip. In return, the person worked for four to seven years without pay. This person was an *indentured servant*. Perhaps half of all Europeans who came to the colonies before 1776 came this way.

Life as a servant was hard. Masters could whip servants and add years for running away. Many died of fever before their time was up. But the contract had an end. When the years were done, the servant was free. Some got land, tools or a new suit of clothes.

Here is the key difference. An indentured servant's contract ended. Slavery did not. By 1700, colonial laws said enslaved people were property for life, and their children were too. Both groups worked without pay. Only one group had a way out.

words.d: a contract to work for someone for a set number of years, often to pay for a trip
a person who worked without pay for years to pay for their passage to America

look.title: The Contract
look.text: Picture a young man in London in 1720. He cannot find work. A captain offers a deal: a free trip to Virginia, food and a bed, and after five years, freedom and fifty acres. He cannot read the paper. He makes his mark with an X. The ship leaves in the morning.
look.prompt: Why might he sign? What risks is he taking? How is his deal different from what happened to Cato's grandmother?

check.q: What did an indentured servant get in exchange for years of work?
check.why: Someone paid the servant's passage across the ocean. The servant repaid it with years of unpaid labor.

check.q: About how many years did an indenture usually last?
check.why: Most contracts ran four to seven years. Then the servant was free.

check.q: What was the biggest difference between an indentured servant and an enslaved person?
choices: Enslaved people only worked in cities
A servant's contract ended; slavery lasted for life and passed to children
check.why: Both worked without pay, but only the servant's time had an end.

lessons.title: The Middle Passage
lessons.mainIdea: Millions of Africans were forced across the Atlantic in chains, and hundreds of thousands were brought to the colonies.
reading: Cato's grandmother was taken from West Africa. Traders marched captured people to the coast and sold them to ship captains. The ocean voyage was called the *Middle Passage*. It was the middle leg of a trade route between Europe, Africa and the Americas.

Below deck, people were chained side by side with barely room to turn. The trip took about two months. The air was foul. Disease spread fast. Roughly one in six or seven people died before reaching land. Ship records kept by the traders themselves tell us these numbers.

Over about three hundred years, roughly twelve million Africans were forced onto ships. Most went to Brazil and the Caribbean. About four hundred thousand were brought to what became the United States. Olaudah Equiano, who was taken as a boy in the 1750s, later wrote a book about it. His words are one of the few accounts we have from someone who survived the voyage.

words.d: the forced ocean voyage of enslaved Africans from Africa to the Americas
forced to work for someone as property, with no pay and no freedom to leave

look.title: A Survivor Remembers
look.text: Olaudah Equiano wrote that when he was carried aboard the ship, he was sure he was going to be killed. Below deck, he said, the heat and the crowding were almost unbearable, the air was hard to breathe, and the cries of the sick and dying made the whole scene one of horror.
look.cite: Olaudah Equiano, from his life story, published 1789 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why is a first-person account like this so important for understanding history? What can it tell us that a ship's record cannot?

check.q: What was the Middle Passage?
choices: The forced ocean voyage of enslaved Africans to the Americas
The trip of indentured servants from England
check.why: The Middle Passage was the middle leg of the Atlantic trade, carrying captured Africans in chains.

check.q: How do we know how many people died on slave ships?
choices: From records kept by the traders themselves
check.why: Ship captains kept careful records of their human cargo. Historians use those records.

check.q: Why is Olaudah Equiano's book valuable to historians?
choices: He drew the first maps of Africa
It was the longest book of its time
It is a rare account by someone who survived the voyage
check.why: Very few people who were enslaved were able to write their stories. Equiano's is one of the few we have.

lessons.title: Town Meetings and Assemblies
lessons.mainIdea: Colonists began governing themselves through town meetings and elected assemblies.
reading: In New England, the men of a town gathered in the meetinghouse for a *town meeting*. They voted on roads, schools, fences and taxes. Anyone could speak. Decisions were made by majority vote. Town meetings still happen in some New England towns today.

Each colony also had an *assembly*, a group of elected men who made laws for the whole colony. Virginia's assembly, the House of Burgesses, first met in 1619. It was the first elected lawmaking body in the colonies. Assemblies decided how tax money was spent. That gave them real power.

Who could vote? Mostly white men who owned land. Women could not vote. Enslaved people and most free Black people could not. Native people could not. Still, more colonists could vote than people in most of Europe. This habit of self-rule would matter a great deal when Britain started to push.

words.d: a gathering where the people of a town vote directly on local decisions
a group of elected people who make laws for a colony or state

look.title: Vote on the Bridge
look.text: The creek floods every spring. At the town meeting, a farmer stands up. He wants a new bridge. A shopkeeper says it costs too much. The blacksmith says his wagon nearly tipped in the creek last week. Hands go up. The bridge passes, eleven votes to seven. The town clerk writes it down.
look.prompt: Who got to raise a hand in this meeting? Who did not? Whose voice was missing?

check.q: What happened at a New England town meeting?
check.why: Town meetings let the men of a town vote directly on roads, schools and taxes.

check.q: What was the House of Burgesses?
choices: Virginia's elected assembly, the first in the colonies
check.why: The House of Burgesses first met in 1619 and made laws for Virginia.

check.q: Who could usually vote in the colonies?
choices: Mostly white men who owned land
check.why: Voting was limited to white men with property. Women, enslaved people and Native people were left out.

lessons.title: A Faraway King
lessons.mainIdea: Britain ruled the colonies but mostly left them alone, so colonists got used to running things themselves.
reading: London was three thousand miles away. A letter took six weeks or more to cross the ocean. The king sent a *governor* to most colonies, but the governor could not do much without the assembly, which controlled the money. Many governors just tried to get along.

Britain cared most about trade. Laws said colonists should ship goods on British ships and sell certain crops only to Britain. But there were few officials to enforce this. Smugglers sneaked in sugar and tea from other countries. Britain mostly looked the other way. Historians call this *hands-off* rule.

For about a hundred years, this worked. Colonists thought of themselves as loyal British subjects with British rights. They also thought of themselves as people who made their own laws. When Britain later tried to tighten its grip, colonists were shocked. They had grown up free of it.

words.d: the leader of a colony, usually chosen by the king
leaving people alone to run things themselves

look.title: How Far Was the King?
look.prompt: If a ship took six weeks to reach London, how long would it take to ask a question and get an answer? What does that mean for who really made decisions?

check.q: Why could a royal governor not do much on his own?
choices: The king did not trust him
Colonists could not read his orders
check.why: Assemblies decided how tax money was spent, so governors needed their cooperation.

check.q: What did Britain care most about in the colonies?
check.why: Britain wanted the colonies to trade with Britain. It paid little attention to daily life.

check.q: Why were colonists shocked when Britain later tightened control?
choices: They had never heard of Britain
They had spent a hundred years mostly governing themselves
check.why: A century of hands-off rule made colonists used to making their own laws.

review.q: Which region grew mostly grain and was called the breadbasket?
review.why: Deep soil in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware grew huge crops of wheat and corn.

review.q: Why did New England turn to fishing and shipbuilding?
choices: Rocky soil, rich seas and tall forests made it the smart choice
review.why: Geography shaped the choice: poor farmland but great fishing and lumber.

choices: A crop grown to feed animals
A crop that grows in cold weather
A crop grown in a city
review.why: Tobacco, rice and indigo were grown for sale, not for the farmer's own table.

review.q: How did an indentured servant's life differ from an enslaved person's?
choices: The servant's contract ended after some years; slavery lasted for life
review.why: Both worked without pay, but only the indenture had an end date.

choices: The forced voyage of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic
The trip of Puritans to Massachusetts
review.why: The Middle Passage was the middle leg of the Atlantic trade that carried captured Africans in chains.

choices: Every family to own a hornbook
Towns with fifty families to hire a teacher
Every town to build a harbor
review.why: This law, driven by the Puritan wish to read the Bible, started public schooling in the colonies.

review.q: Who could vote in most colonial assemblies?
choices: Mostly white men who owned land
review.why: Voting was limited by sex, race and property.

review.q: What does hands-off rule mean for the colonies?
choices: Britain mostly let colonists govern themselves
Britain sent soldiers to every town
review.why: Distance and a focus on trade meant Britain left daily government to the colonists.
